newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Skirmishes block food aid for starving Liberians.
newsitem.headline: Skirmishes block food aid for starving Liberians.

text.p: Food aid destined for thousands of starving people in western Liberia has been held up at Monrovia port for the fourth day because of militia skirmishes in the area, aid workers and militia leaders said on Tuesday.
International aid agencies have not been able to deliver food aid to Tubmanburg town or its outlying famine-stricken districts since Saturday when gunmen turned back convoys.

Guerrillas of the ULIMO-J militia of General Roosevelt Johnson twice blocked food convoys reaching suspected famine areas in Cape Mount County beyond Tubmanburg. ULIMO-J gunmen cited skirmishes between them and rival ULIMO-K fighetrs.
"We haven't gained access to Cape Mount and the food convoys are still waiting to be moved in the area," said spokesman Kent Page of the U.N. Department for Humanitarian Affairs.

Relief workers discovered thousands of skeletal, pot-bellied children and old people in Tubmanburg a week ago after striking a deal with rival factions to enter the town, 70 km north west of Monrovia, for the first time since February.
Hundreds of hungry civilians emerged from the jungle along the road from Monrovia to Tubmanburg. Aid workers said many more were reportedly converging on the town itself.
ULIMO-J officials said in Monrovia on Tuesday clashes were continuing on highways in the area.
"These things would happen but I can assure you they would not degenerate," General Johnson told Reuters, adding that commanders from both sides would meet to resolve the problem.
Aid convoys would only start moving into the area after field commanders had been briefed on the need to respect a peace accord signed by the rival ULIMOs on September 6.

"We are calling them to Monrovia to inform them that we are serious with what we signed. We will allow the relief people in but I think we have to do a little more with our own people," Johnson added.
His reconciled rival, ULIMO-K leader Alhaji Kromah, said on Monday his men left highways after the September 6 deal.
"One commander, perhaps without the knowledge of his leadership or in gross disregard of the agreement, is causing the problems in Cape Mount," Kromah said in a statement.

Aid workers said they were negotiating with ULIMO-J to be allowed to take food to an estimated 35,000 people. The ethnic Krahn dominated ULIMO-J is the strongest group in the area where it battled African peacekeepers last January.
Civil war has killed well over 150,000 people in Liberia, which freed American slaves founded in 1847.

A peace deal clinched in August 1995 fell apart in April and May when faction fighting and an orgy of looting by rampaging gunmen killed hundreds of people in Monrovia. West African leaders brokered a new deal in August and threatened individual sanctions against any faction leader who derailed it.

Under the deal, faction gunmen are to be disarmed by January with elections to follow in May. Kromah's guerrillas turned over heavy weapons just over a week ago at a ceremony intended to mark the genuine start of disarmament.
The latest clashes do not appear to be a serious threat to the relaunched peace process, peacekeepers say.
